nodes.title: Kubernetes pod design (CKAD): Key Ideas
nodes.content: CKAD tests how well you can design pod specs that handle real-world requirements: multi-container collaboration patterns, init container sequencing, resource quotas that prevent noisy neighbors, and probes that give Kubernetes correct signals about pod health. These translate directly to exam tasks where you write or modify YAML under time pressure.

flashcards.front: Multi-container pod patterns — sidecar, adapter, ambassador.
flashcards.back: Sidecar: augments the main container — common uses are log shipping (fluentd reads the app log file) and service mesh proxies (Envoy). Adapter: transforms output from the main container to a standard format — e.g., converts proprietary metrics to Prometheus format. Ambassador: proxies outbound requests from the main container to an external service — handles retries, service discovery, circuit breaking. All three share network namespace and volumes within the pod.

flashcards.front: Init containers — what makes them different from regular containers?
flashcards.back: Init containers run to completion sequentially BEFORE any app containers start in the pod. They are perfect for setup tasks: waiting for a database to be ready, seeding a config file into a shared volume, running a DB migration. Each init container must succeed (exit 0); if one fails, Kubernetes restarts the pod. App containers don't start until all init containers have completed — this is the ordering guarantee regular containers don't provide.

flashcards.front: Resource requests vs limits — what does each do?
flashcards.back: Request: the minimum guaranteed CPU/memory reserved for the container on a node — the scheduler uses requests to decide if a node has enough room. Limit: the maximum the container is allowed to use — if it exceeds the CPU limit it is throttled; if it exceeds the memory limit the container is OOM-killed. Always set both: without requests, the scheduler can over-pack nodes; without limits, one misbehaving pod can starve the whole node.

flashcards.front: Liveness probe vs readiness probe — what does Kubernetes do differently for each?
flashcards.back: Liveness probe: if it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container — used to detect deadlocks or frozen processes. Readiness probe: if it fails, Kubernetes removes the pod from the Service endpoints so no traffic is routed to it — but does NOT restart it. Used to signal 'I'm not ready to serve traffic yet' (warming up cache, loading model). A pod can fail readiness but pass liveness and simply sit out of rotation until it's ready.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

nodes.title: Troubleshooting methodology: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.
